## Does a point lie on a line? {#fv4-point-test .fv-lesson .relation-lesson }

```{=html}
<p>Substitute the point’s coordinates. <strong>One value of <span data-math="\lambda"></span> must satisfy all three equations.</strong></p>
<div class="relation-demo-line"><span data-math="\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}+\lambda\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{bmatrix}"></span><span data-math="\Longrightarrow\quad x=2+\lambda,\quad y=-1+2\lambda,\quad z=1-\lambda"></span></div>
<div class="relation-point-demo">
  <div class="relation-test-on">
    <h3>Test <span data-math="P(4,3,-1)"></span></h3>
    <p><span data-math="x=4\quad\Rightarrow\quad\lambda=2"></span></p>
    <p>With <span data-math="\lambda=2"></span>:</p>
    <div class="relation-test-working"><span data-math="y=-1+2(2)=3"></span><span data-math="z=1-2=-1"></span></div>
    <p class="relation-test-conclusion"><span data-math="P"></span> lies on the line.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="relation-test-off">
    <h3>Test <span data-math="Q(4,3,0)"></span></h3>
    <p><span data-math="x=4\quad\Rightarrow\quad\lambda=2"></span></p>
    <p>With <span data-math="\lambda=2"></span>:</p>
    <div class="relation-test-working"><span data-math="y=-1+2(2)=3"></span><span data-math="\color{#ad6e32}{z=1-2=-1\ne0}"></span></div>
    <p class="relation-test-conclusion"><span data-math="Q"></span> does not lie on the line.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet §3.3 · p. 51 · Additional worked demonstration</div>

::: {.notes}
Connect to Lesson 3: each parameter value gives one position vector, pointing to one point on the line. Use one coordinate to find a candidate parameter, then check every remaining coordinate with that value. For P, x=4 gives λ=2; this also gives y=3 and z=−1, so P lies on the line. Q has the same x and y coordinates, but at λ=2 the line has z=−1 rather than 0. There is no different parameter that can repair z while keeping x=4, so Q does not lie on the line. The deliberately matched x and y coordinates show why checking only two coordinates is insufficient in 3D. This demonstration is additional, not a booklet example; students then apply the method to Example 3.9. If a direction component is zero, its coordinate is constant and the point must have that coordinate; use a non-zero component to find the parameter. In 2D, check both coordinates.
:::
